alalal-e78836-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 6: whether demons believe, and whether their faith is in the practical or speculative intellect.

alalal-e78836-d1e120.summary: Introduces the question on Lombard's (Augustine's) statement that another faith is that of demons, for the demons believe and tremble.

alalal-e78836-d1e134.summary: First objection: unformed faith is of itself capable of being formed, but demons are in no way apt to be formed by grace.

alalal-e78836-d1e151.summary: Second objection: unformed faith is a gift of the Holy Spirit, which does not belong to demons.

alalal-e78836-d1e164.summary: Third objection: unformed faith produces servile fear, which makes one flee sin; this does not fit demons.

alalal-e78836-d1e180.summary: Fourth objection: where would demons' unformed faith come from? Before the fall they knew in the Word, which is not faith and was lost; God is unlikely to have infused faith after the fall.

alalal-e78836-d1e200.summary: Fifth objection: faith is knowledge through mirror and enigma, but angels, good or bad, know through concreated species.

alalal-e78836-d1e213.summary: Sed contra: demons do not know in the Word; they know the articles either by reason, which would make faith demonstrable, contrary to the saints, or by faith; otherwise they would know nothing of the articles, which is false.

alalal-e78836-d1e242.summary: Second sed contra: in Mark 1:24 the demon says 'I know who you are, the Holy One of God', which came neither from rational proof nor from contemplation of the Word, so from faith.

alalal-e78836-d1e261.summary: Raises a further question, because of differing opinions: whether demons' faith is in the practical or affective intellect or in the speculative.

alalal-e78836-d1e272.summary: Introduces arguments that it is in the speculative intellect.

alalal-e78836-d1e279.summary: First argument: demons have no affection for what they believe, and every habit in the affective intellect is affected toward its object, so their faith is in the speculative intellect.

alalal-e78836-d1e292.summary: Second argument: the devil's will is always evil (Augustine), so it never assents to the creed, one of the best things in life; demons believe under compulsion, and only the speculative intellect is compelled.

alalal-e78836-d1e316.summary: Sed contra: demons believe and tremble (James 2:19), so trembling follows their belief; no motion follows the speculative intellect, any more than when we look at terrible things in pictures; so their belief is in the practical intellect.

alalal-e78836-d1e347.summary: Second sed contra: De anima III says the speculative intellect does not move and says nothing about what to flee or pursue, so the faith by which demons tremble is not speculative, as some have said.

alalal-e78836-d1e371.summary: Solution: the saints say demons have faith, but Albert thinks it is not the unformed faith of living humans but a credulity arising from natural knowledge. Though demons lost contemplation in the Word, they kept natural knowledge, by which they know God through effects and conjectures from his works as creator, judge and rewarder; Dionysius says their natural gifts remain intact and brilliant. Augustine ascribes unformed faith to demons by likeness of act and effect, since it causes trembling without turning from sin. So the first arguments stand: demons lack unformed faith, though they have a similar credulity.
claims: Demons do not have unformed faith but a credulity arising from their intact natural knowledge.
Augustine calls it demonic faith by likeness, since it produces trembling without turning from sin.

alalal-e78836-d1e441.summary: Reply to the sed contra: demons' knowledge is neither a remnant of vision in the Word, as unformed faith is in some sense a remnant of formed faith, nor infused after the fall; it results from knowledge of God through experience, effects, miracles and judgments, and natural cognition.
claims: Demonic belief arises from experience of God's works, miracles and judgments together with natural knowledge.

alalal-e78836-d1e463.summary: This also answers the following argument from Mark 1:24.

alalal-e78836-d1e470.summary: On the further question: demons' credulity is not in the speculative intellect, since nothing speculated as such moves one to tremble, but in the practical intellect, which has no will for what is believed but contempt for it, though experience forces them to believe; the practical intellect concerns not only the desirable but also the terrible, from which fear and flight follow.
claims: Demonic belief is in the practical intellect, concerned with what is to be feared.

alalal-e78836-d1e496.summary: To the worry that the articles could then be proved: it does not follow, since a persuasion from effects suffices for such trembling, and, per Avicenna, all practical intellect proceeds from probable premises about what is done by or around us.
claims: Demonic belief rests on a posteriori persuasion, which does not amount to proof of the articles.

alalal-e78836.summary: Article 6 asks whether demons believe, as Lombard says, and whether their belief is in the speculative or practical intellect. Objections argue that demons cannot have unformed faith, since it is formable, a gift of the Spirit, and productive of servile fear, and has no plausible origin in them. On the other side, demons know the articles, which reason cannot prove, as their confession of Jesus shows. Albert holds that demons do not have the unformed faith of living humans. They have a credulity arising from their intact natural knowledge and from experience of God's effects, miracles and judgments. Augustine calls it faith by likeness, since it causes trembling without turning from sin. Because it makes them tremble, it resides in the practical intellect, which bears on the terrible as well as the desirable, though their will scorns what they believe. This a posteriori persuasion does not amount to a proof of the articles.
claims: Demons do not have unformed faith but a similar credulity based on natural knowledge and experience.
Demonic credulity resides in the practical intellect, since it produces trembling.
Demonic belief rests on persuasion from effects and does not prove the articles of faith.
